Contemporary Doenjang-Gochujang Lamb Shoulder

Lamb is the newest voice at this grill — absent from the old lists, fully at home in the modern pantry — and it asks for the two pastes at once: doenjang for the savory floor, gochujang for the red heat, honey to hold them…

Korean · Medium · Serves 4–6

Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary. Lamb is the newest voice at this grill — absent from the old lists, fully at home in the modern pantry — and it asks for the two pastes at once: doenjang for the savory floor, gochujang for the red heat, honey to hold them together against lamb's big flavor. This is a butterflied shoulder steak record: marinated long, grilled hot in thick slices, served ssam-style with the sharp fresh salads that lamb and the Korean table both love. No lineage claimed — this one is written for the cook who wants the Korean grill's flavors on the meat their butcher is proudest of this week.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The two pastes must be worked smooth together before anything else joins — doenjang and gochujang are both stiff and will not dissolve on their own. Whisk them with the soy, honey, and sesame oil into a uniform rust-colored paste, then the aromatics and the squeezed pear.
  • Marinate 8–24 hours, refrigerated. Lamb shoulder is a thick, working muscle; the long window is not optional, and the pear's enzyme work is doing half the tenderizing. Reserve a third of the marinade before the meat goes in as the finishing brush.
  • Plan the fire two-zone: medium-hot for searing the slices, a cool corner for the pieces that color faster than they cook.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Slice the marinated shoulder across the grain into strips 2 cm wide. Sear in a single layer on the medium-hot zone — lamb's fat wants to flare, so the grill boss stays at the grate with tongs, moving strips to the cool corner when their edges catch. Checkpoint — the strips should sear to a deep brown-red crust with light char at the fat edges, and the smell should be the pastes toasting over rendered lamb fat — rich enough that the table will ask what it is before it is ready.
  2. 02
    Work in batches, brush as each batch finishes: cook each strip until a food thermometer in the thickest part reads at least 145 °F (63 °C), then brush the hot strips with the marinade reserved before contact with raw lamb. Cooking time varies with thickness and heat. Checkpoint — a test strip at the grill station: a browned crust, and the pastes' savory-heat arriving behind the lamb's big flavor rather than on top of it. If the marinade reads louder than the meat, the strips were thin or the marinade thick — the meat is the headline at this table.
  3. 03
    Rest the batches 3 minutes on a warm platter as they come off, sesame over, and the platter goes to the table's center for ssam service: perilla leaf, a swipe of ssamjang (#SA01), a hot strip, a piece of pickled perilla or onion, fold, one bite. Checkpoint — the ssam test: the perilla's anise edge against the lamb's richness with the pickled cut through the fat is the record's finished thought — rich, sharp, herbal, one bite. If the wrap collapses into pure richness, the pickle was skipped; it is load-bearing here. Chef’s Note — why the two pastes together: doenjang alone on lamb runs magnificent but one-note deep; gochujang alone runs sweet-hot and lets lamb's gaminess through the back door. Together, the fermented-soy floor and the chile's fruit close over the lambiness from both sides — the same reason a jjigae pot holds both. Lamb simply happens to be the protein that makes the pairing most obvious.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Flare-ups consuming stripsLamb fat over open flameTwo-zone fire; cool corner discipline
Marinade louder than lambOver-thick coat or thin stripsReserve the brush for the finish only; 2 cm strips
Chewy slicesWith-grain cut or short marinateAcross the grain; the full 8 hours minimum
Pastes stayed lumpyNot whisked smooth firstDoenjang + gochujang + liquids to uniform before aromatics

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated shoulder keeps 24 hours, freezes 1 month. Cooked, 3 days — leftover slices into a gimbap-style roll or a rice bowl with the last reserved marinade warmed as sauce.
  • Variations: the same marinade on lamb chops (shorter marinate, 4 hours); beef short rib takes this paste beautifully for a nontraditional weeknight galbi (#M03's cut, this record's flavor); mushroom caps in the reserved marinade grill alongside for the table's vegetarians.
